items.stem: Two angles are corresponding angles between parallel lines. One of them is 46°. What is the other angle?
items.markingKey: Corresponding angles equal: 46°. [1]

items.stem: Two lines are crossed by a transversal. A pair of corresponding angles are 43° and 45°. Leila says the two lines are parallel. Explain why Leila is wrong.
items.answer: If the lines were parallel the corresponding angles would be equal. They are not equal, so the lines are not parallel.
items.markingKey: B1 corresponding angles equal for parallel lines; B1 conclusion. [2]

items.stem: Lines AB and CD are parallel, with A and C on the left. A straight line EF crosses AB at P and CD at Q, with E above AB and F below CD. Angle APQ = 67°. Kenji says angle CQP is also 67° because they are alternate angles. Explain the mistake and give the correct size of angle CQP.
items.answer: APQ and CQP are on the same side of the transversal, between the parallel lines: they are co-interior, so they add up to 180°. CQP = 113°.
items.markingKey: B1 identifies co-interior (not alternate); B1 180° − a. [2]

items.stem: Lines AB and CD are parallel, with A and C on the left. A straight line EF crosses AB at P and CD at Q, with E above AB and F below CD. Angle APQ = 42°. Work out the size of angle CQF. Give a reason for your answer.
items.answer: 42°; corresponding angles (with angle APQ)
items.markingKey: B1 42°; B1 reason: corresponding angles (with angle APQ).

items.stem: Lines AB and CD are parallel, with A and C on the left. A straight line EF crosses AB at P and CD at Q, with E above AB and F below CD. Angle APQ = 51°. Work out the size of angle BPQ. Give a reason for your answer.
items.answer: 129°; angles on a straight line add up to 180°
items.markingKey: B1 129°; B1 reason: angles on a straight line add up to 180°.

items.stem: Lines AB and CD are parallel. Triangle PQR has P on AB and both Q and R on CD, with Q to the left of R. Angle APQ = 45° and angle BPR = 43°. (a) Work out angle PRQ, giving a reason. (b) Use your answers to explain why the angles in a triangle add up to 180°.
items.answer: (a) 43° (alternate with angle BPR) (b) Angles APQ, QPR and BPR lie on the straight line AB so add to 180°; APQ = PQR and BPR = PRQ (alternate), so the three angles of the triangle add to 180°.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 value; B1 reason [2] (b) B1 straight line; B1 alternate angles [2]

items.stem: Which pair of angles between parallel lines are equal and form a Z shape?
items.answer: Alternate angles
items.markingKey: Alternate angles lie on opposite sides of the transversal, between the parallels. [1]

items.stem: Two lines are crossed by a transversal. A pair of corresponding angles are 105° and 107°. Diego says the two lines are parallel. Explain why Diego is wrong.
items.answer: If the lines were parallel the corresponding angles would be equal. They are not equal, so the lines are not parallel.
items.markingKey: B1 corresponding angles equal for parallel lines; B1 conclusion. [2]

items.stem: Explain how you can use corresponding angles to show that two lines are parallel.
items.answer: Measure (or calculate) a pair of corresponding angles; if they are equal, the lines are parallel.
items.markingKey: B1 corresponding angles; B1 equal implies parallel. [2]

items.stem: Lines AB and CD are parallel, with A and C on the left. A straight line EF crosses AB at P and CD at Q, with E above AB and F below CD. Angle APQ = 35°. What is angle EPA?
items.markingKey: EPA = 145° (angles on a straight line (EPQ) add up to 180°). [1]

items.stem: Two parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. A pair of alternate angles are (3x + 6)° and (2x + 30)°. Find x and the size of each angle.
items.answer: x = 24; each angle is 78°
items.markingKey: Alternate angles are equal: 3x + 6 = 2x + 30 (M1); collect terms: x = 24 (M1); x = 24 (A1); angle = 3 × 24 + 6 = 78° (A1).

items.stem: Two parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. A pair of alternate angles are (5x + 40)° and (4x + 54)°. Find x and the size of each angle.
items.answer: x = 14; each angle is 110°
items.markingKey: Alternate angles are equal: 5x + 40 = 4x + 54 (M1); collect terms: x = 14 (M1); x = 14 (A1); angle = 5 × 14 + 40 = 110° (A1).

items.stem: Lines AB and CD are parallel, with AB above CD. A point X lies between the lines. Angle ABX = 50° and angle XDC = 56°, where B and D are both on the right of X. Draw a line through X parallel to AB and use it to work out angle BXD. Give reasons.
items.markingKey: Line through X parallel to AB splits angle BXD into 50° (alternate with ABX) [2] and 56° (alternate with XDC) [2]; total 106° [1].

items.stem: What is the sum of the interior angles of a decagon?
Can a regular polygon have interior angles of 100°? Give a reason.
items.answer: No: exterior angle = 80° and 360 ÷ 80 = 4.5, not a whole number.
items.markingKey: M1 finds exterior angle and divides into 360; A1 conclusion. [2]

items.stem: Sofia says the interior angles of a hexagon add up to 6 × 180° = 1080° because it can be split into 6 triangles. Explain the mistake and give the correct total.
items.answer: Joining one vertex to all the others splits the hexagon into 4 triangles, not 6, so the sum is (6 − 2) × 180° = 720°. (Splitting from a centre point gives 6 triangles but the 360° at the centre must be subtracted.)
items.markingKey: B1 explains n − 2 triangles (or subtract 360°); B1 correct total. [2]

items.stem: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 45°. How many sides does the polygon have?
Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 36°. How many sides does the polygon have?
Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 60°. How many sides does the polygon have?
Tariq draws a regular pentagon. (a) Work out the size of one exterior angle. (b) Work out the sum of the interior angles.

A tile is in the shape of a regular pentagon. (a) Work out the size of one interior angle. (b) Explain whether regular pentagons will tessellate on their own. (c) Two vertices next to each other are joined to the centre of the pentagon. Work out the angle at the centre.
items.answer: (a) 108° (b) No: 360 ÷ 108 = 3.333, not a whole number, so they leave gaps. (c) 72°
items.markingKey: (a) M1 180 − exterior; A1 [2] (b) M1 360 ÷ interior angle; A1 conclusion [2] (c) B1 360 ÷ n [1]

items.stem: What is the sum of the interior angles of a hexagon?
What is the sum of the interior angles of a quadrilateral?
Explain why the interior angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360°.
items.answer: A diagonal splits the quadrilateral into two triangles, each with angle sum 180°, so the total is 2 × 180° = 360°.
items.markingKey: B1 two triangles; B1 2 × 180. [2]

items.stem: Grace says it is possible to draw a regular polygon with an exterior angle of 25°. Is Grace correct? Explain.
items.answer: No: 360 ÷ 25 = 14.4, which is not a whole number, so it cannot be the number of sides.
items.markingKey: M1 360 ÷ exterior angle; A1 conclusion about whole number of sides. [2]

items.stem: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is 144°. Work out the number of sides.
6 of the interior angles of a heptagon are 122°, 159°, 127°, 135°, 122°, 109°. Work out the size of the remaining angle.
4 of the interior angles of a pentagon are 127°, 114°, 147°, 107°. Work out the size of the remaining angle.

A regular decagon and a regular octagon are placed side by side so they meet at a point with no overlap. (a) Work out the angle needed to fill the gap at the point. (b) Could the gap be filled exactly by the interior angle of another regular polygon? If so, how many sides does it have?
items.answer: (a) 81° (b) No: no regular polygon has that interior angle.
items.markingKey: (a) M1 360 − 144 − 135; A1 81° [2] (b) M1 exterior = 180 − 81; M1 360 ÷ exterior; A1 conclusion [3]

items.stem: Hana draws a regular hexagon. (a) Work out the size of one exterior angle. (b) Work out the sum of the interior angles. (c) Explain whether regular hexagons will tessellate on their own.
items.markingKey: (a) M1 360 ÷ n; A1 [2] (b) M1 (n − 2) × 180; A1 [2] (c) M1 360 ÷ interior angle; A1 conclusion [2]

items.stem: What is true about every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB?
options: It is the same distance from A and from B
It lies on the line AB
It is twice as far from A as from B
It is closer to A than to B
items.answer: It is the same distance from A and from B
items.markingKey: Definition of the perpendicular bisector. [1]

items.stem: When constructing the perpendicular bisector of AB, explain why the compasses must be set to more than half the length of AB.
items.answer: If the radius is half AB or less, the arcs from A and B will not cross (or will only touch on AB), so there are no two points to join.
items.markingKey: B1 arcs must intersect; B1 reason with half AB. [2]

items.stem: Explain why the compass width must stay the same for both arcs when constructing a perpendicular bisector.
items.answer: The crossing points must be the same distance from A and from B; with equal radii they are, so they lie on the perpendicular bisector.
items.markingKey: B1 equal radii; B1 equidistant points. [2]

items.stem: A is the point (7, 5) and B is the point (9, 5). Write down the equation of the perpendicular bisector of AB.
items.markingKey: Midpoint of AB = (8, 5) (M1); AB is horizontal so the bisector is vertical: x = 8 (A1).

items.stem: A is the point (1, −1) and B is the point (1, 9). Write down the equation of the perpendicular bisector of AB.
items.markingKey: Midpoint of AB = (1, 4) (M1); AB is vertical so the bisector is horizontal: y = 4 (A1).

items.stem: On a coordinate grid, a tree stands at T(1, 2) and a well at W(1, 10). A treasure is buried at a point that is the same distance from T and W, and the same distance from the x-axis and the y-axis (in the first quadrant). (a) Write down the equation of the perpendicular bisector of TW. (b) Explain which two constructions you would use to find the treasure on a map.
items.answer: (a) y = 6 (b) The perpendicular bisector of TW and the bisector of the angle between the axes.
items.markingKey: (a) M1 midpoint (1, 6); A1 y = 6 [2] (b) B1 B1 [2]

items.stem: What is true about every point on the bisector of angle ABC?
options: It is the same distance from A and C
It is closer to B than to A
It lies on the line AC
It is the same distance from the lines BA and BC
items.answer: It is the same distance from the lines BA and BC
items.markingKey: The angle bisector is the locus of points equidistant from the two arms. [1]

items.stem: Sofia says that point X is on the perpendicular bisector of BD because XB = 4 cm and XD = 5 cm. Explain whether Sofia is correct.
items.answer: No. Points on the perpendicular bisector are equidistant from B and D; XB ≠ XD, so X is not on it.
items.markingKey: B1 equidistant property; B1 conclusion. [2]

items.stem: Explain why joining the two crossing points of equal arcs from A and B gives a line perpendicular to AB.
items.answer: The four points A, B and the two crossing points form a rhombus (all sides equal radius); the diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles.
items.markingKey: B1 rhombus; B1 diagonals perpendicular bisectors. [2]

items.stem: A is the point (1, −2) and B is the point (1, 8). Write down the equation of the perpendicular bisector of AB.
items.markingKey: AB is vertical; midpoint has y = 3. [1]

items.stem: Describe how to construct the perpendicular bisector of a line AB of length 6 cm, using only a ruler and compasses.
items.answer: Open the compasses to more than 3 cm. Draw arcs above and below AB from A, then with the same radius from B. Join the two points where the arcs cross.
items.markingKey: B1 radius more than half AB (3 cm); B1 equal arcs from A and B; B1 join intersections.

items.stem: Describe how to construct the perpendicular from a point P to a line, where P is 9 cm away from the line.
items.answer: Draw an arc centred at P cutting the line at two points; from these points draw equal arcs that cross on the other side; join P to the crossing point.
items.markingKey: B1 arc from P cutting line twice; B1 equal arcs from the two points; B1 join.

items.stem: Two radio masts, P and Q, are 10 km apart. A phone signal is received from the nearer mast. (a) Describe the line on which the signal is equally strong from both masts. (b) A house is 6 km from P and 5 km from Q. Which mast does it receive its signal from? (c) Describe the region of points that are within 6 km of P and closer to Q than to P.
items.answer: (a) The perpendicular bisector of PQ. (b) Mast P (it is nearer to P). (c) The part of the circle of radius 6 km centred at P that lies on Q's side of the perpendicular bisector.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 perpendicular bisector [1] (b) M1 compare distances; A1 P [2] (c) B1 circle radius 6 km centre P; B1 side of bisector nearer Q [2]

items.stem: Which set of side lengths, in cm, makes a right-angled triangle? 6, 8, 11; 10, 24, 25; 5, 12, 12; 7, 24, 25
Chloe says a triangle with sides 8 cm, 15 cm and 18 cm is right-angled. Use Pythagoras' theorem to decide whether Chloe is correct.
items.answer: 8² + 15² = 289 but 18² = 324. They are not equal, so the triangle is not right-angled.
items.markingKey: M1 compares sum of squares of shorter sides with square of longest; A1 conclusion. [2]

items.stem: Sipho says: "In a right-angled triangle with shorter sides 15 cm and 20 cm, the hypotenuse is 15 + 20 = 35 cm." Explain why this cannot be true.
items.answer: The hypotenuse must be shorter than the sum of the other two sides (triangle inequality). By Pythagoras it is √(15² + 20²) = 25 cm.
items.markingKey: B1 reason; B1 correct value. [2]

items.stem: Triangle XYZ has a right angle at Y. The hypotenuse XZ = 15 cm and XY = 9 cm. Calculate the length of YZ.
items.answer: 12 cm

items.stem: Triangle ABC has a right angle at B. AB = 14 cm and BC = 5 cm. Calculate the length of AC, giving your answer to 1 decimal place.
Triangle XYZ has a right angle at Y. The hypotenuse XZ = 13.7 cm and XY = 7.1 cm. Calculate the length of YZ, correct to 1 decimal place.

A rectangular park is 60 m by 80 m. Diego walks from one corner to the opposite corner. (a) Calculate the distance saved by walking along the diagonal instead of along two sides. (b) Walking at 1.5 m/s, how many seconds does the diagonal route take?

A television screen is a rectangle 80 cm wide and 45 cm high. (a) Calculate the length of the diagonal of the screen, to the nearest centimetre. (b) Screen sizes are given in inches (1 inch = 2.54 cm). Work out the screen size to the nearest inch. (c) Calculate the area of the screen.
items.answer: (a) 92 cm (b) 36 inches (c) 3600 cm²

items.stem: In a right-angled triangle, which side is the hypotenuse?
options: Any side next to the right angle
The side opposite the right angle
items.answer: The side opposite the right angle
items.markingKey: The hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the 90° angle. [1]

items.stem: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 5 cm and another side 3 cm. Ana works out the third side as √(5² + 3²) = 5.8 cm. Explain the mistake and find the correct length.
items.answer: The missing side is shorter than the hypotenuse, so subtract: √(5² − 3²) = √16 = 4 cm.
items.markingKey: B1 should subtract for a shorter side; B1 correct length. [2]

items.stem: Explain how to use Pythagoras' theorem to check whether a triangle with sides 9 cm, 12 cm and 15 cm is right-angled.
items.answer: 9² + 12² = 81 + 144 = 225 = 15², so the triangle is right-angled (the converse of Pythagoras).
items.markingKey: M1 squares of the two shorter sides added; A1 compared with longest side squared. [2]

items.stem: Explain why the hypotenuse is always the longest side of a right-angled triangle.
items.answer: c² = a² + b² is bigger than a² and bigger than b², so c is bigger than a and b.
items.markingKey: B1 c² is the sum of two positive squares; B1 conclusion. [2]

items.stem: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 15 cm and another side 9 cm. Mohammed works out the third side as √(15² + 9²) = 17.5 cm. Explain the mistake and find the correct length.
items.answer: The missing side is shorter than the hypotenuse, so subtract: √(15² − 9²) = √144 = 12 cm.
items.markingKey: B1 should subtract for a shorter side; B1 correct length. [2]

items.stem: Calculate the distance between the points (4, 4) and (13, −8).
items.markingKey: Horizontal 9, vertical 12 (M1); √(9² + 12²) = √225 (M1); 15 (A1).

items.stem: Triangle XYZ has a right angle at Y. The hypotenuse XZ = 13 cm and XY = 5 cm. Calculate the length of YZ.
items.answer: 12 cm

items.stem: A television screen is a rectangle 112 cm wide and 63 cm high. (a) Calculate the length of the diagonal of the screen, to the nearest centimetre. (b) Calculate the area of the screen.

A rectangular park is 60 m by 80 m. Kwame walks from one corner to the opposite corner. (a) Calculate the distance saved by walking along the diagonal instead of along two sides. (b) Walking at 1.5 m/s, how many seconds does the diagonal route take? (c) Explain why the diagonal is always shorter than the two sides added together.
items.answer: (a) 40 m (b) 66.7 s (c) The straight line is the shortest path; in a triangle any side is shorter than the sum of the other two.

items.stem: Which pair of angles between parallel lines add up to 180°?
items.answer: Co-interior angles
items.markingKey: Co-interior (allied) angles form a C or U shape. [1]

items.stem: Explain why co-interior angles add up to 180°, using alternate angles.
items.answer: One co-interior angle and its neighbour on the straight line add to 180°; that neighbour equals the other co-interior angle (alternate angles), so the co-interior angles add to 180°.
items.markingKey: B1 straight line; B1 alternate angles. [2]

items.stem: Lines AB and CD are parallel, with A and C on the left. A straight line EF crosses AB at P and CD at Q, with E above AB and F below CD. Angle APQ = 77°. Work out the size of angle PQD. Give a reason for your answer.
items.answer: 77°; alternate angles (with angle APQ)
items.markingKey: B1 77°; B1 reason: alternate angles (with angle APQ).

items.stem: Lines AB and CD are parallel. Triangle PQR has P on AB and both Q and R on CD, with Q to the left of R. Angle APQ = 61° and angle BPR = 75°. (a) Work out angle PQR, giving a reason. (b) Work out angle PRQ, giving a reason.
items.answer: (a) 61° (alternate with angle APQ) (b) 75° (alternate with angle BPR)

items.stem: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 20 cm and another side 12 cm. Diego works out the third side as √(20² + 12²) = 23.3 cm. Explain the mistake and find the correct length.
items.answer: The missing side is shorter than the hypotenuse, so subtract: √(20² − 12²) = √256 = 16 cm.
items.markingKey: B1 should subtract for a shorter side; B1 correct length. [2]

items.stem: Ravi says a triangle with sides 9 cm, 40 cm and 42 cm is right-angled. Use Pythagoras' theorem to decide whether Ravi is correct.
items.answer: 9² + 40² = 1681 but 42² = 1764. They are not equal, so the triangle is not right-angled.
